t: Are You Making Your Most Difficult Students Worse? -worse/
q: But this awareness can cause you to behave oddly around them.

Because when you act differently around difficult students than you do the rest of your class, you’re effectively telling them that they’re not like other students, that they’re incapable of being trusted and that you expect them to misbehave.
They know when they’re being surveilled, marked, and followed. They know when they’re disliked and resented—or merely tolerated.
The solution, however, is simple: From the very first moment of each school day onward, you’re going to pretend that your most difficult students are already well behaved.
That isn’t to say that they’ll never again misbehave, but they’ll no longer do it to spite you or get under your skin.
Their burden will lift. They’ll look you in the eye, unashamed. And for the first time in their school career, they’ll relax into their skin.

q: Her words had power because she praised him in a way that mattered to him, in a way that sparked his intrinsic motivational engine. And this makes all the difference.

Any and all praise you offer your students must be based on truth. It must be in response to real accomplishment rather than a self-interested desire to placate , flatter, or manipulate the student into behaving.
She steadfastly refused to lower the bar of excellence in her classroom by engaging in false praise and “caught being good” manipulation.
The more impressive the accomplishment, the more important it is to pull the student aside to offer your praise.
And contrary to the oft-repeated advice that praise must always be immediate, giving your students a moment or more to enjoy their successes before jumping in can be much more powerful.
If a student performs a routine, direction, task, or procedure as taught, then a simple ‘thank you’ will do.
If, however, you witness performance that is truly noteworthy, then speak from the heart. Make your praise genuine.

q: You catch a student in the act of misbehavior and you move in to redirect them.
Well, because it’s done while the student is in the act of misbehavior , it encourages an argumentative response.
You see, whenever you try to stop misbehavior while it’s occurring, you increase the likelihood of a confrontation—particularly with difficult students.
The chief reason for this is that redirection doesn’t allow your students to reflect on their mistakes.
It’s best to let the misbehavior play out , to continue with whatever you’re doing while keeping an eye on the student.
The calm clarity of the message, combined with your quick exit from the scene, causes the student to automatically contemplate their violation of class rules.
The best part, though, is that there is no confrontation, no resentment, and no added disruption to your teaching.
x: Redirecting a student mid-misbehavior invites argument, justification, and a defensive reaction.
He explains that correcting a student mid-misbehavior encourages them to explain away or justify their actions and puts the teacher at risk of losing composure.
Letting misbehavior play out, then delivering the consequence afterward, produces less confrontation and more accountability.

The deeper problem, he argues, is that immediate redirection prevents students from reflecting on their own mistakes, which reduces the odds they take real responsibility and increases the odds of repeat misbehavior.
His alternative is to let the misbehavior play out fully, then approach only once it's finished and deliver a calm, brief consequence before walking away.
A calm, brief, factual consequence statement followed by a quick exit avoids drawing the teacher into debate.
Linsin challenges the instinct to physically intervene and redirect students the moment misbehavior is spotted, arguing it invites arguments and defensiveness.

t: Why Caring Too Much Can Make You A Less Effective Teacher -effective-teacher/
q: And when you care too much, not only are you wrung out, preoccupied, and no fun to be around, but you make mistakes that make you a less effective teacher.
You become personally offended when students misbehave. You become irritable, easily frustrated, and less approachable.
The truth is, the most effective teachers maintain a level of professional distance—from their students, their classroom, and even their school.
You see, when you take on what are your students’ responsibilities, even emotionally, they’ll be left with the message that they have a free pass.
Your job is to teach, inspire, and hold accountable—which is completely in your control.
Your students will feel the burden of responsibility for learning and behaving settle upon their shoulders, where it belongs.
x: Effective teachers maintain professional distance and treat teaching as a two-way street with clearly separated responsibilities.

Linsin warns that over-investing emotional identity in teaching can backfire, making teachers irritable, easily offended by misbehavior, and prone to taking over responsibilities that belong to students.
Effective teachers maintain professional distance and treat teaching as a two-way street with clearly separated responsibilities.
Absorbing students' responsibilities emotionally signals to students that accountability is optional.
A teacher's three core responsibilities are to teach, inspire, and hold accountable—full stop.
Handing the remaining responsibility for learning and behavior back to students restores balance and reduces teacher stress dramatically.
